case_study_insert.main_stem: Hartwell Community Pharmacy (HCP) is a private limited company in the healthcare retail sector, dispensing prescriptions and delivering medicines to local care homes across the city, and employing a workforce of 27. Founded in 2008 by Margaret Ellison, the business operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HCP plans to invest $450,000 in an automated dispensing robot and a home-delivery hub, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 34,000 units a year, measured in items dispensed. HCP faces stubbornly high dispensing errors and lengthy customer-waiting times at its counter.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2026: The pharmacy dispensed 8,450 items last quarter with a dispensing error rate of 0.4%, down from 0.9% a year ago. Complaints about counter waiting times fell from 22 to 14 per month. Average prescription wait is 18 minutes. A survey of 480 customers found that 73% want a repeat-prescription reminder service and 61% would use a home-delivery service. Eight of 27 staff require accuracy-checking certification; off-the-job training at the pharmacy college costs $520 per employee. HCP is piloting a medicine take-back and recycling scheme for unused medicines.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Hartwell Community Pharmacy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans and overdrafts. (2) Wholesale medicine prices have risen 10.5% year-on-year as manufacturers increase costs. (3) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.55 to $13.35 per hour from April 2026, while consumer spending on health and wellness products grew 4.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HCP plans to finance part of its dispensing robot with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HCP of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs HCP nothing in interest or repayments at a time when the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, making new variable-rate borrowing markedly dearer. It protects cash flow against the 10.5% rise in wholesale medicine prices, which is already straining working capital, and avoids committing the pharmacy's steady but regulated prescription income to a lender.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps ownership and control with Margaret Ellison and existing shareholders, with no bank covenants over stock levels, margins or the home-delivery hub. It avoids interest on top of fixed costs already standing at $168,000 a year, preserves loan capacity for future regulatory or equipment changes, and signals to the local community and care-home partners that HCP is a financially resilient independent — valuable reputation capital for winning delivery contracts.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Community Pharmacy and its dispensing expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HCP is launching its new home-delivery service for medicines. Consider local radio sponsorship, community health-fair sponsorship, or a social media campaign. Which should HCP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio sponsorship: Local radio would reach a broad cross-section of HCP's catchment — commuters, retired listeners and care staff — repeatedly and cheaply. It suits reminder-style messages such as the 73% who want a repeat-prescription reminder service. However, airtime is untargeted, half the audience will never order a delivery, and younger decision-makers who arrange care for elderly relatives are poorly reached by local AM/FM formats.

Community health-fair sponsorship: Health fairs put HCP directly in front of exactly the people the home-delivery service serves — elderly patients, unpaid carers, care-home managers and GP surgery staff. Trust transfers from the event to the pharmacy, demonstrations of the delivery process reassure nervous patients, and partnerships with care homes can produce bulk contracts. The weakness is limited scale: one event per month touches only a few hundred people.

Social media campaign: A targeted campaign reaches the adult children and carers who usually arrange medicines for elderly relatives, pushes the home-delivery message to thousands, and drives measurable sign-ups at low cost. However, HCP's core patients are older and less active on social platforms, so conversion relies on family intermediaries and creative execution.

Recommendation: HCP should choose community health-fair sponsorship. It reaches the highest-intent audience with the greatest trust, directly previewing the service for care-home decision-makers and the 61% of customers who said they would use home delivery. Local radio is rejected as too broad and weakly targeted for a niche service; social media alone is rejected as a primary channel because HCP's end users are older and sceptical online, though a small paid campaign aimed at carers should support the fairs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HCP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HCP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and social media are rejected as the primary channel.

questions.question_text: HCP's dispensing errors and counter waiting times concern its pharmacy team. Explain two benefits for HCP of democratic leadership when motivating its staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 27 staff — dispensers, accuracy checkers, counter teams and drivers — into designing the reminder service and delivery routes, satisfying their esteem needs and building genuine ownership of clinical quality. Staff who help shape procedures are more vigilant, which directly attacks the 0.4% error rate and supports the fall in waiting-time complaints from 22 to 14 per month.

Point 2: Involving staff surfaces practical fixes managers would never see — for example splitting the 18-minute average wait with a dedicated collection counter, or staggering delivery rounds around care-home medication times. Consultation also deepens commitment among dispensers and counter staff, protecting the 34,000 items dispensed a year and cutting the $520 per employee cost of repeated accuracy-checking certification.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HCP's errors, waiting times and delivery expansion.

questions.question_text: HCP wants to cut dispensing errors further. Consider installing the automated dispensing robot with off-the-job training for 8 staff or improving accuracy through on-the-job coaching and revised procedures. Which should HCP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Automated dispensing robot with off-the-job training: The robot physically prevents the most common mis-picks, standardises counting for high-volume repeat prescriptions, frees staff for clinical checks and care-home deliveries, and produces an audit trail — critical as the delivery service scales. Off-the-job certification at $520 x 8 = $4,160 gives recognised accuracy credentials. Drawbacks are the $450,000 capital cost, installation disruption and residual errors at the final clinical check, which still needs humans.

On-the-job coaching and revised procedures: Coaching by senior dispensers is nearly free, immediate and tailored to HCP's actual error patterns — the 0.9%-to-0.4% fall shows recent gains. It requires no downtime investment. However, manual systems remain error-prone under pressure at the 18-minute-wait counter, produce no capacity for the 61% home-delivery demand, and create no audit-grade evidence for care-home contracts.

Decision: HCP should choose the automated dispensing robot with off-the-job certification, funded within the $450,000 expansion. Errors and capacity are the twin constraints on growth: a robot prevents repeat mis-picks at machine level while coaching only manages human inconsistency, and coaching alone cannot unlock the delivery contracts HCP is courting. On-the-job coaching is rejected as the sole solution, though it remains essential afterwards for the final clinical safety check on every robot-prepared prescription.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to HCP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of HCP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of HCP with a well-justified decision covering safety, capacity and delivery ambitions.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HCP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $168,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $168,000 ÷ $6.00 = 28,000 items. Answer: break-even output is 28,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HCP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 28,000-unit break-even with 34,000 items dispensed shows a margin of safety of 6,000 units, signalling that the $450,000 robot and delivery hub can be serviced with headroom before volumes slip.
2. Contribution data lets HCP price the home-delivery service: charging $2 per delivery lifts effective contribution on delivered items to $8.00, so managers can forecast exactly when the hub turns profitable and whether to bundle free delivery above a basket threshold.
3. Unit cost data — ($168,000 ÷ 34,000) + $8.00 = $12.94 per item — lets managers benchmark counter performance, spot waste in packaging for the delivery trial and renegotiate wholesaler terms amid the 10.5% wholesale price inflation.
4. Labour productivity of 34,000 ÷ 27 = about 1,259 items per employee lets managers roster dispensers versus drivers, identify where waiting times peak, and target the eight staff needing accuracy-checking certification at the busiest shifts.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 28,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,000 units versus 34,000 items produced; delivery-fee pricing modelling for the 61% home-delivery demand; unit-cost benchmarking at $12.94 against the 10.5% wholesale inflation; and productivity targets of about 1,259 items per employee to roster the delivery hub.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HCP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HCP's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 32.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 9.2%
Profit Margin 2025 = 13.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 19.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $615,000 on revenue of $2,050,000 (615 ÷ 2,050 = 30.0%); 2025 gross profit $768,000 on revenue of $2,400,000 (768 ÷ 2,400 = 32.0%). Operating profit rose from $189,000 (189 ÷ 2,050 = 9.2% of revenue) to $312,000 (312 ÷ 2,400 = 13.0% of revenue). With capital employed of $1,050,000 in 2024 and $1,600,000 in 2025, the return on capital moved from 189 ÷ 1,050 = 18.0% to 312 ÷ 1,600 = 19.5%. Revenue grew $350,000 (17.1%) while cost of sales grew only $197,000, reflecting the delivery service and reminder-driven repeat business.

Evaluation: Performance has improved across all three measures, though the capital-hungry expansion diluted the return on capital employed — capital employed leapt $550,000 while the return rose only 1.5 percentage points. Interest payable climbed from $40,000 to $55,000 as debt levels rose. The 10.5% wholesale medicine inflation will test the 32.0% margin in 2026, and the 6.4% minimum wage rise will lift wage costs; however, the 4.6% consumer spending growth on health products and the 73% reminder-service demand underpin repeat revenue.

Conclusion: HCP's financial performance has improved — profitability (30.0% to 32.0%), operating margin (9.2% to 13.0%) and return on capital employed (18.0% to 19.5%). The improvement is real and broad-based, and home delivery should deepen it, but HCP must defend margins through supplier renegotiation, strict dispensing accuracy via the robot, and disciplined labour scheduling as wage and medicine inflation build.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether HCP's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: HCP is piloting a medicine take-back and recycling scheme for unused medicines. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HCP of introducing this scheme.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A take-back scheme positions HCP as a responsible community pharmacy, strengthening trust with care homes, GP surgeries and environmentally conscious families — reinforcing the repeat-prescription reminder service demanded by 73% of customers and supporting council health partnerships that competitors cannot easily replicate. It also differentiates HCP from chains and supports CSR objectives at near-zero marketing cost.

Disadvantage: Secure collection, storage and lawful disposal of controlled medicines carry real costs — licensed waste contracts, storage cabinets, staff time and record-keeping — raising the $168,000 fixed-cost base and potentially the $520 per employee certification burden. Poor handling could breach regulations and damage HCP's licence to operate, and uptake may disappoint, leaving stranded disposal capacity and admin overhead for years before recycling contracts mature.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HCP's community role, regulations and customer research.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 10.5% rise in wholesale medicine prices and the 6.4% minimum wage increase will affect HCP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): HCP's $250,000 variable-rate loan costs roughly 0.75% more a year — about $1,875 — plus higher overdraft charges on working capital drawn to fund stock. Interest payable already rose from $40,000 to $55,000 in the latest extract. The impact is real but absorbable within $312,000 of operating profit, and HCP can hedge by negotiating a fixed rate or repaying from trading surplus.

Wholesale medicine inflation (10.5%): Medicine purchases dominate cost of sales ($1,632,000). National reimbursement tariffs typically lag price movements, so on the non-reimbursed and OTC component — say $400,000 of own-choice sales — a 10.5% rise adds roughly $42,000 a year. More broadly, it squeezes cash tied up in stock, strains supplier credit terms and risks out-of-stocks if HCP cannot fund larger orders before the robot frees capacity.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.35): HCP's counter, delivery and admin teams include many near-minimum-wage roles. On 15 eligible staff averaging 1,950 hours, the current wage bill is about 15 x $12.55 x 1,950 = $367,000; a 6.4% rise adds roughly $23,500 a year, hitting just as HCP recruits drivers for the delivery hub.

Conclusion: The 10.5% wholesale medicine inflation will have the greatest impact. It adds roughly $42,000 of direct margin pressure — more than the wage rise ($23,500) and more than twelve times the interest increase ($1,875) — and its effect compounds through stock cash requirements across a $1,632,000 medicine spend. HCP should renegotiate wholesaler rebates and payment terms, automate replenishment through the robot, and protect OTC pricing, while absorbing the wage rise through rostering and modest service-fee adjustments on the delivery hub.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HCP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HCP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HCP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
